en: Regarding the meaning of the Ten Doors of Non-duality:
this Trace Gate discusses cause and effect as well as self and other, so that the teachings of the entire lifetime of the Buddha may be harmonized and enter the Subtle.
Therefore, all explanations of these meanings rely upon the Four Teachings and the Five Flavors, with the intent that the teachings be opened up so that all may enter [the ultimate truth].

The contemplation of the mind as the "cream of cream" (*paramānanda*) is the pivotal mechanism of the teaching and practice; however, for the time being, it shall be briefly indicated by way of various expositions.

Whether it is preserved or omitted, this is not the primary intent of the specific school; thus, even if there are established arrangements, they are merely incidental to the Dharma, or consist of enumerating the names of the ten contemplations.

What is clarified here concerns the principles, objects, wisdom, practices, stages, and dharmas—both the transformer and the transformed—and the intention regarding the expressive capacity of the means of expression (*vyañjana*).

The "Middle" [chapter] is profoundly subtle in its discernment and exposition of the internal beginning and end, as well as self and others; thus, it fully elaborates the ten subtleties (*daśa-prakāra-sūkṣmatā*) to encompass the entire purport of the world-transcending teaching, leaving nothing unexhausted.
Therefore, one must not fail to understand the Great Sūtra through these ten subtleties. Herein, the ten subtleties are summarized as the general framework for the method of contemplation.

If one understands the subtlety of the traces (*traces-subtlety*) and the subtlety of the source (*source-subtlety*), they are not remote; one should know that they are merely matters of separation and integration.

The meanings of "difference" (*bhinna*) and "identity" (*eka*) regarding cause and effect—how could self and other be distinct? Therefore, the text below states: "Though the origin (*hon*) and the trace (*saku*) differ, they are inconceivably one.

Furthermore, since essence, doctrine, and function are merely the phenomena of self, other, cause, and effect, how much more so is the aspect of the teaching (*kyō-sō*) merely a differentiation of the preceding four chapters?
If one understands this principle, then the preceding four chapters will be forever distinguished from other texts. If one realizes this intent, then...

The teachings have a single point of convergence; whether viewed vertically or horizontally, they do not transcend the three thousand worlds within a single thought-moment. From the principle and realm of emptiness, provisionality, and the middle, down to the benefits for others—all are thus.

Consequently, the ten stages of practice in *śamatha-vipaśyanā* constitute the cause and effect of one’s own cultivation (*svacaryā*), while the chapter on "Arising the Teachings" constitutes the subject and object of transforming others (*paracaryā*).
Thus, when these aspects mutually illuminate one another, the practice of the *Lotus Sūtra* is perfected, ensuring that one's efforts are not in vain.
Since that which is expressed [by these teachings] can be understood, they are not in vain; therefore, the ten mysteries (*daśa-prakāra-guhyam*) are further subsumed under ten gates.
What are these? Granting the provisional based on the real makes the non-dual dual; revealing the real by opening the provisional makes the dual non-dual.

Since both the Dharma and the teaching sections are thus opened to become mysteries, these ten gates are titled "Non-Duality. Under each gate, one should examine them through the six stages of realization (*ṣaḍ-bhūmi*).

The preceding text has extensively cited authentic evidence; hereafter, I shall directly set forth a single principle so that the purport of this entire scripture may appear vividly before one's eyes.
These are: first, the gate of the non-duality of form and mind; second, the gate of the non-duality of the internal and external;
third, the gate of the non-duality of cultivation and nature; fourth, the gate of the non-duality of cause and effect; fifth, the gate of the non-duality of defilement and purity; sixth...

The seventh is the gate of the non-duality of the primary and the secondary; the eighth is the gate of the non-duality of self and others; the ninth is the gate of the non-duality of the three karmas;
the tenth is the gate of the non-duality of receiving and moistening. Among these, the first establishes its name based on the excellence of the object;
the second and third establish their names based on wisdom and practice; the fourth establishes its name based on the dharma of the stages; and the fifth...
The sixth and seventh [sections] are named according to the supernatural powers of response; the eighth and ninth are named according to the teaching of the Dharma;
and the tenth is named according to the benefits for the retinue. Regarding the "Gate of the Non-duality of Matter and Mind":

from the ten suchnesses of objects up to the ultimate truth, each possesses both a general and a specific meaning. The general meaning resides in a single thought-moment, while the specific meaning is divided into matter and mind.

Regarding the first ten aspects (*lakṣaṇa*): their characteristics reside solely in form (*rūpa*), while their nature resides solely in the substance of mind; their function as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) encompasses both mind and form.

Their cause and effect reside solely in the mind, while their retribution (*vipāka*) pertains solely to form. Regarding the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*): suffering and karma pertain to both, while afflictions (*kleśa*) reside solely in the mind. Regarding the four noble truths (*catuḥ-satya*):

three [truths] encompass both form and mind, while cessation (*nirodha*) resides solely in the mind. Regarding the two truths (*dvi-satya*) and the three truths (*tri-satya*), all are conventional (*saṃvṛti*) and complete.

Within the true reality of form and mind, there is only the single reality of Mind-only, which is without external reference; this is what can be seen. Once one knows these distinctions, one integrates the particular into the universal:
among all dharmas, there is nothing that is not the nature of mind. This single nature is "no-nature," wherein the three thousand worlds are perfectly manifest.

One should know that the form and mind of the mind are themselves the mind; they are called "transformation" (pariṇāma) and "creation" (nirmāṇa). Because their essence is identical, they are not [mere] form.
It is neither mind nor form, yet it is both mind and form; that it is "only form" and "only mind" is precisely due to this.

Therefore, one knows that consciousness alone, in a single thought-moment, universally perceives oneself and others, as well as past and future lives and other Buddhas. Since these are identical to the mind, how could the mind of oneself and the Buddha of the mind ever diverge?
For this reason of the single thought-moment, the various phenomena of those respective objects differ yet do not differ. Second, the Gate of the Non-duality of Internal and External: Whatever...

Contemplating the object, one finds it does not transcend the internal or the external; that is to say, by relying upon those [phenomena] of the environment and its inhabitants, form and mind, they are immediately empty and immediately the Middle.

Because emptiness and the Middle are subtle, the essence of mind and form is severed, leaving only the single true nature. Without emptiness, the provisional, or the Middle, yet form and mind appear vividly, suddenly identical with true purity.
There are no longer the distinctions of sentient beings or the seven stages of the expedient means; one sees no differences between pure and impure lands, for all are sovereign.

The net of the dependent and the primary realms culminates in what is called "resplendent clarity. As for that which is called "internal," one first realizes that external forms and the mind are, in a single thought-moment, devoid of discursive thought;

there is only the internal essence of the three thousandfold world, which is itself empty, provisional, and middle. Thus, external phenomena are entirely the nature of the mind, and since the nature of the mind has no exterior, its encompassing is all-pervasive.
The Dharma-realm of the Buddhas of the ten directions and the essential nature of sentient beings are no different; all are entirely so.

Regarding the question of who pervades all, it is said that internal and external form and mind—whether belonging to oneself or others—are established by means of the aforementioned "Gate of the Non-duality of Form and Mind.

Third, regarding the "Gate of the Non-duality of Cultivation and Nature": the nature-merit is simply the *dharmadhātu* (the suchness of the realm) within a single thought-moment. This internal *dharmadhātu* is fully endowed with the three dharmas;

although its nature is thus from the beginning, it is called "cultivation" when it relies upon wisdom. Through cultivation, one illuminates the nature; through the nature, cultivation is manifested. Thus, cultivation exists within the nature.

Thus, when cultivation is perfected, nature arises; when cultivation proceeds from nature, cultivation is perfected by nature. Nature does not shift, yet cultivation remains ever manifest. Furthermore, there are two kinds of cultivation:

cultivation in accordance with [nature] and cultivation in opposition to it. "In accordance" means realizing nature as one's practice; "in opposition" means turning one's back on nature to become deluded.

Although these two minds—realization and delusion—are non-dual, the two natures of accord and opposition are always distinct in their phenomenal manifestations. This is because, while the principle is not different, the phenomena are distinct.

If one shifts the mind, it causes confusion regarding cultivation, realization, completion, and fulfillment; therefore, throughout a single period, one must clarify the nature through delusion and fulfill cultivation through realization.

When seeing the nature and cultivating the mind, both types of cultivation are extinguished. Furthermore, one must understand that cultivation accords with the nature, wherein there is both separation and union.

"Separation" means that cultivation and nature each have three aspects; "union" means that the two aspects of cultivation and the one aspect of nature together give rise to the three aspects of nature. Thus, although cultivation—*
The nine times nine are merely three; these are established as pairs in order to clarify cultivation in relation to the nature.

Thus, cultivation is combined into two pairs and one nature, like water being waves. These two are neither two nor distinct, just as waves are water. One should know that "nature" refers to the three obstacles;

therefore, the three cultivations are complete. From the nature, they are perfected; the three dharmas are thus realized as non-cultivation. In nature, there is only the single wondrous vehicle, wherein nothing exists.

The thorough illumination of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) is accomplished through the gate of the non-duality of the internal and external. Regarding the fourth, the gate of the non-duality of cause and effect:
since the cause—the mind of sentient beings—already possesses the three tracks (trivartman), the fruit produced by this cause is called the three nirvāṇas.

There is no distinction between cause and fruit; from beginning to end, the principle is one. If this is so, why does the cause not abide in its own virtue? It is solely because of delusion regarding the cause that [sentient beings] differ.

One considers oneself to have truly realized it; yet, because the nature of delusion is fundamentally real, one merely abides in the cause. Having long investigated this cause, when the cause is manifested, it is called the fruit.
Precisely because the principle of cause and fruit is one, by employing this single principle as the cause, once the principle is manifested, the name "fruit" no longer exists.

How could the designation of "cause" still persist? Since both cause and fruit have vanished, the rational nature itself is extinguished. It is solely due to the proximity or distance of the wisdom of extinction that [these distinctions arise].
Delusion becomes thick or thin; because delusion is thick or thin, the three afflictions are forcibly distinguished, and their meanings are opened into six levels according to the depth of wisdom.
Thus one knows that through diligent application of effort, the emptiness of names cuts off delusion. Since the illusory cause is fulfilled, the mirror-image fruit is perfected.

Although the empty image and the [empty] principle are identical in meaning, the emptiness is void while the image is real; therefore, it is called the "fundamental emptiness of principle," for delusion is void.

When nature is transformed into this state, duality is established within non-duality, such that cause and effect are distinct yet non-dual; though beginning and end appear separate, their essence is one.
If one claims the cause differs from the effect, then the cause is not truly a cause; it is only by understanding that the effect arises from the cause that the cause can then produce the effect.

Thus, the three thousand realms existing in the principle are collectively termed "ignorance," while the three thousand realms when the fruit is realized are all called "eternal bliss"; the three thousand realms undergo no change.

Ignorance (*avidyā*) is itself enlightenment; the three bodies (*trikāya*) are both eternally identical in essence and identical in function. This is established through the gate of the non-duality of cultivation and nature.

Regarding the fifth, the gate of the non-duality of defilement and purity: if one realizes that from the beginningless past ignorance has been the very nature of the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), then it can be understood that now ignorance itself is the nature of the Dharma.
This ignorance of the Dharma-nature universally creates all phenomena; this is termed "defilement."
The dharma-nature of ignorance pervades all conditions; it is designated as turbid water or clear water.
The waves and moisture are no different, yet clarity and turbidity arise through conditions. Although turbidity is originally present, its entire substance is fundamentally clear.

Because the principle of the two waves applies universally—that the whole substance is both essence and function—the three thousandfold world of cause and effect is collectively termed "dependent origination" regarding both delusion and enlightenment.
The principle of dependent origination does not depart from the nature of moment-to-moment arising;

within each and every principle of this single dependent origination, one distinguishes between the pure and the defiled—specifically, six are defiled and four are pure. Yet, in their universal sense, all ten penetrate both the pure and the defiled.

Thus, we know that although the essence of the defiled moments is entirely pure, because the three thousand realms have not yet been manifested and verified, the essence remains obscured by delusion; therefore, at the stage of semblance, the six sense organs achieve universal illumination.

The division into ten realms each possesses its own distinct clarity; how could it be that those with pure six sense organs claim the ten realms are fixed as ten or that the ten realms of manifested traces are likewise fixed?

This is because they are established through fruition as being equal to those hundred realms. Therefore, from the very first moment of the Bodhisattva path, one must employ both cessation (*śamatha*) and illumination (*vipaśyanā*):
because of illumination, the three thousand [realms] are eternally present; because of cessation, they are by nature empty. Ultimately, they are both absent and ultimately, they are both manifest.

Without moving from this thought, one responds universally to all directions; bestowing according to the stimulus, purity and impurity both vanish. Because one forgets purity and impurity, one employs emptiness and the mean.

Furthermore, by means of emptiness and the mean, one transforms defilement into purity. Through the realization that defilement and purity are inherently extinguished within emptiness and the mean, the "Gate of the Non-duality of Cause and Effect" is thereby established.
Sixth, regarding the "Gate of the Non-duality of the Dwelling Place and its Inhabitants": having already realized the *śūnyatā* (one-ness) of the Dharma-realm...
The non-duality of essence arises precisely because from beginningless time, the three thousand realms are contained within a single thought-moment.

Within these three thousand, two thousand realms constitute the sentient beings (the "correct" realm), while one thousand realms belong to the environment (the "reliance"). Since both the correct and the reliant reside within each and every thought-moment, how could subject and object be divided?

Although there is no subject or object, the distinction between the reliant and the correct remains manifest. Thus, in the stage of the true nature, the names, and the practice of contemplation, non-duality is already perfectly established.

Based on these characteristics, the causes and effects of self and others are mutually inclusive. Although sentient beings have not yet manifested the fruit in principle, everything without exception is none other than the wondrous realm of Samantabhadra (*Cakrasaṃvara*).

Nevertheless, one must further understand that the essence of the Buddha-dharmas is pervasive though not [merely] all-pervasive, and the rational nature of sentient beings is non-localized yet remains unchanged from beginning to end;
thus, there is no hindrance between the Great and Small Vehicles, and the principles of cause and effect are identical.

Since there is no distinction between the primary [body] and its environment, why would there be pure and impure lands, superior and inferior bodies, or a difference between the *rūpakāya* and the *dharmakāya*?

If the dimensions of the *rūpakāya* and the *dharmakāya* are identical, and if the *rajas-kṣetra* (dusty lands) and the *śānta-prabhāsvara* (tranquil light) are no different, then every single atom-particle land is all lands, and every single atom-particle body is all bodies.
Their breadth and narrowness, their superiority and inferiority, are inconceivable; their pure and impure locations are inexhaustible. This is not [the case] unless one possesses the three [bodies].
How could the thousandfold emptiness, the provisional, and the middle establish such sovereign function?

Only through this can one know that the arising of Buddhas and sentient beings, as well as the phenomena and principle of self and other, mutually encompass one another; this is accomplished by way of the gate of the non-duality of defilement and purity. Seventh, regarding the gate of the non-duality of self and other:

the act of benefiting others according to their capacities relies upon the fundamental nature—that is, the single nature is inherently complete—and it is only upon reaching the stage of fruition that self and other are fully realized.
Self-benefit and benefiting others are like the three virtues and three truths of the principle-nature;

the three thousand [realms] of self-cultivation exist solely within emptiness, while the three thousand realms of benefiting others respond to the infinite capacities of beings. Though the modes of response are manifold, they do not transcend the three thousand;

though the ten realms manifest and transform one another, they do not transcend a single thought-moment. The lands arise mutually, yet they do not transcend the serene light; sentient beings likewise [arise from it].

Because the principle (*li*) inherently possesses the three thousand [realms], it is able to move all Buddhas; because the principle of the three thousand is fulfilled, it is able to respond universally to every capacity.
If it were not thus, how could it be like a mirror manifesting images? The mirror possesses the principle of manifesting images, and the form possesses the nature of generating an image.
If a single form were unable to produce an image when facing the mirror, then the principle of the mirror would be exhausted, and the reality of the form would be deficient.

If one has not yet attained penetration, there may indeed be the principle that a mirror can be separated [from its object]; however, there is no form that faces a mirror and does not produce a reflection.

If a mirror fails to manifest a reflection because it is obscured by dust, removing the dust depends on a person’s polishing, yet the manifestation of the reflection itself is not dependent on the act of polishing. By means of this analogy, the general purport of contemplating the Dharma can be understood.

One should know that although the principle is inherently complete within both self and other, it must rely upon the conditions of the *ālambana-pratyaya* (object-condition) and the *hetu-pratyaya* (causal-condition) to become beneficial.

Furthermore, his merit arises only when the conditions (*pratyaya*), the causes (*hetu*), and the nature (*svabhāva*) are unified; only then can he manifest the myriad phenomena in accordance with that nature.

Thus, he does not give rise to a self-nature, and his transformations are without fixed location. This is accomplished through the gate of the non-duality of the environment and its inhabitants (*bhājana-sattva*).

8. The Gate of the Non-duality of the Three Karmas: Within the gate of transforming others, the activities are divided into the three mysteries (*triguhya*). These receive different names in accordance with the principles of things (*dharmatā*). First is the wheel of mind (*citta-cakra*).
The Two Wheels [of the Dharma] reflect sentient beings' capacities, manifesting transformations and preaching the Dharma without the slightest error.
If the two bodies were distinct, why would it be said that they "are themselves the Dharmakāya"? If the two teachings were contradictory, why would it be said that "all shall attain Buddhahood"?
If there were only the Dharmakāya, there would be no manifestation in the world; if there were only...

In the Buddha-way, who bestows the three vehicles? Since the body is ultimately non-existent, even "speaking" is not speaking. Body and mouth are equal; likewise, the mental wheel is identical to the physical form of the mind.
Without deliberation, transformation occurs; one is eternally in accord with the ultimate. Adapting actions to the capacities of beings—how could this not be the single mind within the ten realms?
Within each realm, there is nothing that is not the three karmas. Since even a single thought contains the three karmas, how can the fruition and its function differ?
When the cause is unimpaired, it must correspond to the fruit; only through faith does one know that the three mysteries are primordially present.
Because the three karmas of the hundred realms are simultaneously empty, provisional, and middle, they are made to correspond appropriately and respond universally as the fruit.

Each manifested form and each spoken word is without exception fully endowed with the three karmas of the hundred realms. To manifest further manifestations—this is what is meant by this. Thus, even within a single thought-moment of an ordinary mind...
The ocean of the three mysteries of the rational nature (*dharmatā*) and the retributive form within a single atom are both identical in their fundamental principle;
only when they are Vairocana is this termed "the non-differentiation of the three. This is established through the gate of the non-duality of self and other.

Ninth, the gate of the non-duality of the provisional and the real: the great wisdom of equality constantly contemplates the *dharmadhātu*. Furthermore, by virtue of the rational nature, there are nine provisional aspects and one real aspect; yet these are once again [non-dual].

The provisional nature of the nine realms is likewise so; where the provisional and the real are mutually merged, the hundred realms exist within a single thought-moment, beyond differentiation, spontaneously and eternally as they are.
Upon reaching the fruition, one accords with the fundamental principle of oneness, which is neither provisional nor real, yet both provisional and real. This is just as previously described:

through the sovereign mastery of the mind-wheel, the body and speech respond to the capacities of both the provisional and the real, such that the three karmas do not deviate from a single thought-moment.

Since the provisional and the real are immovable, how could their application be separated or differentiated? When addressed in terms of correspondence, they are designated as "provisional" and "real";
when applied to the person, they are named "True" and "Responsive. The principle of the three karmas is identical: the provisional and the real are in profound union.

This constitutes the gate of the non-duality of the three karmas. Regarding the gate of the non-duality of the ten types of reception and moistening: the nature of dharmas is originally and inherently endowed with the provisional and the real, perfumed from time without beginning.
Practice may be either ultimate or provisional; yet the ultimate and the provisional are always equal through the principle of perfuming (*vāsanā*).

When the opportune moment is met, practice and vows are brought to fruition. If there were no fundamental cause, perfuming would be in vain. While the meeting with perfuming appears diverse, this is not due to any difference in nature.

Although nature has no distinction, it must rely on the manifestation of illusion. Through illusory capacity, illusory resonance, illusory response, and illusory engagement, both the one who responds and those being transformed are not merely provisional.

In reality, because the causes [of Buddhahood] are neither provisional nor real, they constitute the capacity for both the provisional and the real; likewise, the Buddha’s fruition is neither provisional nor real, yet he manifests as the provisional and the real to accord with the capacities of sentient beings.
These responsive bodies and lands are without partiality, identical to the eternal *dharmadhātu* of tranquil light, and there is nothing that is not the *dharmadhātu*.

Therefore, one should know that the three thousand realms are co-present within the mind-ground, and that these three thousand realms in the Buddha’s mind-ground are no different from the substance of the four subtle elements.
Because they are identical, the provisional and the real, as well as their benefits, are equal; this is established through the gate of the non-duality of the provisional and the real.

Therefore, each of the ten gates universally enters into both form and mind, and so on, until all beings are moistened by the Dharma. Thus, the ten wonders (jūmyō) are from beginning to end a single principle.

As the principle is originally inherent in the objective realm, one gives rise to understanding based upon that principle; this is called "wisdom" (chi). Wisdom guides practice, and practice accords with the principle. Third.
The dharmas correspond and are not different, yet they appear as different; thus, "shallow" and "deep" are provisionally established to set up stages and eliminate confusion.
These three dharmas are simply the realization of that principle. Regarding the five chapters following the third [section], these are the arising of the functions of the three dharmas.

Since the three dharmas are already the three thousand in a single thought-moment (*ekacitta-kṣaṇa*), and since the empty, the provisional, and the middle are established, they possess function. If one understands this single thought-moment, one understands the dharmas of all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
Since the fundamental and the phenomenal are not remote from one another, these ten gates are restated so that they may be recognized through contemplative practice.
Since the title is thus, one can understand the general principle by examining the specific details. *The Meaning of the Ten Gates of Non-duality* (concludes).
This punctuated edition was completed on the twenty-eighth day of the sixth month in the first year of the Genjū era, based on a red-ink punctuated manuscript, by the śramaṇa Shinsei (etc.).
The Record of Items Brought from Tāizhō by the Great Master Dengyō states: "One fascicle of the *Jūfunimon-gi*."
The *Record of the Same [Text] from Yue Province* states: *Ten Non-Dual Sections Text*, one fascicle.
The catalog of items brought by Daisōjō (Zhizheng Dashi) states: *Meaning of the Ten Non-Dual Gates*, one fascicle (Miaole).
The catalog of writings composed by various masters states: *Meaning of the Ten Non-Dual Gates*, one fascicle (Master Miaole).
The *Catalogue of Various Sectarian Texts* (compiled by Dharma Master Gen’i by imperial decree in the fourteenth year of the Enkyō era) states:

“*The Meaning of the Ten Non-Dual Gates*, composed by the Preceptor Shikan. The *Catalogue of the Master’s Writings* (recorded by the Preceptor Shuzen) states: “*Collection of the Ten Non-Dual Meanings*, one fascicle.”

Twelve sheets: *Kāoyì* (Examination of Variants), *Shí bù'èrmén yì shì zhūzhǐ* (Pointing to the Pearl Index to the Meaning of the Ten Gates of Non-duality), and *Fǎhuá shímào bù'èrmén zhù* (Commentary on the Ten Profound Mysteries of the Non-duality Gate of the Lotus Sutra). Ten.
The *Fahua benji shibu’ermen zhiyaochao Wenxinjie* and the Mingzang edition both treat the "Ten Non-dual Gates" as an exposition of the Manifesting the Subtle (*xianmiao*).
The *Fahua xuanyi ji* treats the "Ten Non-dual Gates" as an exposition of the Mysterious Record (*xuanyi*).
Now, I say that their meaning is identical to the fourfold Four Truths, the sevenfold Two Truths, and the Three Truths.
In such cases as "the meaning of the four *siddhāntas*," "the meaning of the ten *dharmadhātus*," and so forth, the character "義" (*gi*) cannot be omitted.
However, in this recently printed edition, the character "然" (*nen*) is punctuated to be read [as part of the preceding term], whereas in ancient editions it was not read as "然.

This two-character compound reading of "然此" (*nenni*) is identical to that of the present edition. (Note: The original text contains a circle symbol [○] indicating a gap or a point of emphasis; the translation reflects this structural note.)

Examining this, the rule for its interpretation is as follows: in the *Lunyu*, it appears in the phrases "as if pointing to this" (*ru shi zhu si*) and "this is what is meant by 'this'" (*qi si zhi wei*).
Both the *Guangyun* and the *Longkan Shoujian* state that "ran" (*ran*) is a particle used as an expletive, as in "thus" (*ru*) or "so" (*e*). Furthermore, examining the *Liji*, it says:
"Duke Mu summoned Xianzi and asked him, 'Is it so? (*mu gong zhao xian zi er wen ran yue*). The commentary states: "'Ran' is a word [of affirmation]."
In the first year of the Kasei era, the scholar of the Seiwa Genji clan produced a punctuated edition of the *Riji* (Book of Rites) with interlinear readings;
however, he added a fine note beside the character "於" stating that it is not read.

The *Jiao* commentary (Ten-Volume *Wenxin*): the *Xianmiao Mingben* manuscript copied by Yao; the *Shishu* edition copied during the Kwanhei era; the *Shizhu* edition published as a woodblock during the Kōan era;
the *Shiqian* manuscript copied during the Jōji era; the *Shiqian* movable-type edition from the Genwa era; the *Koben* (classified edition) of the *Shiqian*;
the *Kenshō Sōzu* annotated edition of the woodblock text; and the *Koben* (classified edition) of the *Shiqian* manuscript copied during the Kwan’ei era.
The *Keqian* (Sectional Index) is identical to the present edition.

Regarding the commentary on "mind and form" (*xīn sè*), the ten instances of "manifesting the wondrous clarity" (*xiǎn miàomíng běn*) are all rendered as "form and mind" (*sè xīn*) in the Kuan-hsi edition.
Furthermore, the *Shizhu*, the Song Canon’s *Shiqian*, the *Hongqian*, the *Zhenqian*, and various other editions of the *Keqian* are all identical to the present one.
In the phrase "and the unmanifest, wondrous, wordless," the character *di* (truth) is added below.

Regarding the identity of the essence (*ti*), the *Shiyao* (Essentials), *Wenxin* (Heart of the Text), *Xianmiao* (Manifesting the Wondrous), *Benri* (Original Record), *Yuanji* (Record of Yuan), *Songqian* (Song Commentary), and the editions of Kuanxi and Yongzheng all read "essence and function" (*tiyong*).
The *Shizhu* (Pearl Necklace), Zhu Xiong’s *Chao*, Huikai’s *Tanjue*, and the Japanese editions of the *Ri* [commentary] likewise [support this].
The *Ji*, *Hongqian*, *Zhenqian*, *Keqian*, and various other editions all agree with the present version.

Now, it is said that the subsequent phrases—"the cause and effect are identical," "the principle is identical," and "the four subtle elements are identical in substance"—share the same textual meaning;
thus, the corruption of the term "function" (*zuoyòng*) can be clearly understood.

In the *Jitazhu Shizhiyao* (己他註十指要), the *Wenxin Xianmiaoming Ben* (文心顯妙明本), and the Song-era commentaries (*Songqian*), as well as the *Kuanxi Ben* (寬喜本)—which adds the characters "sentient beings and Buddhas" (*shengfo*) beneath the word "other" (*ta*)—and the *Shizhu Ri* (示珠日), *Zhaohong Qian* (朝弘籤), *Zhenqian* (貞籤), *Keqian* (科籤), and various other editions, all agree with the present text. Since there already exists this excellent original manuscript transmitted from antiquity, upon what basis could the fabrications of later persons be relied upon? Is it not, then, utterly groundless for the *Shiyō* to claim such things?
We have now carved this excellent manuscript and further collated it against various other editions, cross-referencing them all so that right and wrong may be made perfectly clear.
The instances where the Song editions have been interpolated and altered do not end with this work alone;

I have distinguished between the merits and defects of the various ancient, Song, and Ming editions in detail, so that students may open the eye of discernment regarding the Dharma and straighten the needle for attaining the Way. Thus it is said.
